title: Overview of research progress and application of experimental models of colorectal cancer

subsections.section_title: In Vitro Cellular Models of Colorectal Cancer
subsections.content:
In vitro models of CRC established using intestinal cells and CRC cells are frequently employed for obtaining rapidly growing cellular models of CRC and for facilitating experimental control ref [1], ref [2]. In vitro models of CRC can simultaneously generate several populations of homogeneous cells ref [1], ref [2]. Specific cellular targets of macroscopic systems can be conveniently studied using these models by analyzing the experimental results ref [1], ref [2].

The establishment of models using the corresponding tumor cells is crucial for investigating the mechanism underlying the development of CRC and discovery of anti-CRC drugs ref [1], ref [2]. The applications of different cellular models of CRC according to the different molecular mechanisms underlying tumor formation, including epithelial-mesenchymal transition (EMT), apoptosis, invasion, metastasis, chromosome instability (CIN), and immune escape, are summarized in Table 1 and Figure 4 ref [1], ref [2]. subsections.subsection_title: Foundations and Evolution of In Vitro CRC Cell Culture Models
subsections.content: CRC cell lines are in vitro tumor models with different origins and types, and serve as fundamental tools for investigating the biomarkers of drug sensitivity, resistance, and toxicity ref [4], ref [6]. CRC cell lines are established by isolating CRC cells from patients or animals with CRC followed by culture on artificial media ref [5], ref [6]. The appropriate cell lines are selected based on the type of cancer or gene expression levels, according to the aims of the study ref [4]. SW620, Caco-2, RKO, SW480, HT8, HT29, HT116, LoVo, and LS174 T cell lines are currently widely used in basic research studies on CRC ref [4], ref [6].

subsections.section_title: In Vitro Cellular Models of Colorectal Cancer
subsections.content: Owing to the limitations of 2D cellular models of CRC, researchers are committed towards exploiting novel and physiologically representative models of CRC ref [8], ref [11]. In vitro 3D culture models, including spheroids and organoids, are therefore used for overcoming the limitations of 2D cellular models ref [7], ref [8], ref [11]. Spheroids comprise a mixture of single-cell or multicellular systems, while organoids are generally formed of specific stem cells or ancestral cells from organs ref [8], ref [11]. Spheroids and organoids are superior at mimicking tumor cell heterogeneity and the complex interactions among different cells ref [7], ref [8], ref [11]. MCTS models are similar to solid tumors in terms of the growth kinetics, metabolic rate, and resistance to chemotherapy and radiotherapy in vivo ref [8], ref [10], ref [11], and have been employed for screening and evaluating the efficacy of drugs ref [7], ref [8], ref [10], ref [11]. However, the variability of MCTS models makes it difficult to obtain repeatable and stable experimental data, which affects the use of these models in tumor research ref [8], ref [11].

Organoids are typically used for investigating the mechanism underlying the development of CRC, screening anti-CRC drugs, and determining the efficacy and mechanism of action of drugs ref [19] ref [20]. However, there are various limitations to the application of organoids in studies on CRC, which are described hereafter. First, the current methods for organoid culture lack the technological means for maintaining the blood vessels, immune system, and peripheral nervous system of tumor cells, and organoids lacking these characteristics cannot be used in CRC research ref [19]. Second, as PDO models lack the cellular and acellular components of the TME of the original tumor, they cannot equivalently represent the in vivo environment of the tumor ref [19] ref [20]. Third, there are no specific media for culturing organoids to date ref [19]. Furthermore, it is unclear whether organoids can represent the overall heterogeneity of the tumor and all cell types in the tumor ref [19]. Organoids can be applied to relevant studies by optimizing the culture conditions for maintaining the expression of genes related to microsatellite instability, B-Raf proto-oncogene, serine/threonine kinase (BRAF) mutations, poor differentiation, or mucinous phenotypes related to CRC ref [20]. The application of organoids to CRC research can be improved by employing the co-culture model of organoids in which immune cells and mesenchymal cells are co-cultured for simulating the in vivo TME ref [19].

In addition to rodents, invertebrates such as fruit fly can be used for personalized diagnosis and developing potential therapeutic strategies for CRC. Vertebrates such as zebrafish, dogs, cats, pigs, and non-human primates are also used in studies on CRC. The advantages and disadvantages of the different animal models used in CRC research are summarized in Table 3.

subsections.section_title: In Vivo Experimental Animal Models of Colorectal Cancer
subsections.subsection_title: Dietary Risk Factors and Tumor Heterogeneity
subsections.content:
The occurrence of diseases such as cancer that occur spontaneously in animals is largely attributed to genetic diversity and immune functions. Therefore, studying the methods for generating animal models of CRC can aid in elucidating the mechanisms underlying the development of cancer. Animal models can compensate for the limitations of cellular models that are incapable of simulating the mechanism underlying the development of CRC. Rat and murine models are the most frequently used animal models of CRC, and other animal models of CRC, including fruit fly, zebrafish, and pigs, are also commonly used as sentinels and preclinical models in CRC research.

The carcinogenesis of CRC is affected by several contributing factors, including dietary patterns and tumor heterogeneity ref [21]. The selection of the animal model of CRC depends on the purpose of the study, as summarized in Table 4.

subsections.section_title: In Vivo Experimental Animal Models of Colorectal Cancer
subsections.subsection_title: Genetic Basis of Colorectal Tumor Development
subsections.content: Rodent models are conducive tools for conducting cancer research, and are extensively used for elucidating the etiopathogenesis and molecular mechanisms underlying the development of CRC. Previous studies have demonstrated that the protein-coding genes of mice and humans share high homogeneity. Additionally, the use of murine models is advantageous owing to the fact that mice have a short intergenerational interval, high reproducibility, and similar genetic background and formula as humans, compared to other animal models. Murine models of CRC can therefore be used as effective tools for studying the mechanism underlying the pathogenesis of CRC and determining novel strategies for the prevention and treatment of CRC ref [22].

subsections.section_title: Study Design, Synthesis, and Scholarly Apparatus
subsections.content:
Understanding the inherent advantages and limitations of the different models of CRC, and the appropriate application of these models in drug development and studies on the mechanism of tumor occurrence and development are important in CRC research.

Human cell lines and xenograft models have been extensively employed over the past few decades owing to their low cost and ease of application. However, these models are incapable of reproducing the heterogeneity of CRC tumors. The cell coculture technique can overcome the limitations of monolayer cell culture, and enables the construction of in vitro physiological or pathological models that closely represent the in vivo condition, and can be used for studying the interactions between cells, and between cells and the culture environment. It has been reported that 3D models can mimic the physiological characteristics of parental tumors, including tumor heterogeneity. However, the shape, size, and activity of organoids are different under the same culture conditions, and the matrix limits the penetration of drugs and hinders drug screening. It is therefore imperative to construct a model that closely represents the characteristics of CRC in vivo.

The intestinal microarray platforms used in CRC research, which consist of intestinal organoids and organic chips, can summarize the important structural features and functions of the natural duodenum. This platform can be applied for studying drug conveyance, metabolism, and drug-drug interactions. Multi-locus transfer chips consist of multiple 3D organoids that connect the CRC-like organs, liver, lungs, and endothelial flow via recirculating fluid systems, and enables cell tracking by fluorescence imaging technology. The transfer sites of CRC cells are also included in multi-locus transfer chips.

Animal models of CRC have been widely used for studying the complexity of CRC ref [23]. There are primarily two types of animal models, namely, in situ models and the cell and tissue transplantation models of CRC ref [23]. Owing to the relatively simple modeling approach of human tumor xenotransplantation, this model is presently widely used for studying the efficacy of anti-CRC drugs ref [30]. The effects of CRC xenotransplantation can be closely related to clinical activity via the rational application of these models ref [30]. For instance, genetically engineered murine models have been used for studying the progression of tissue-specific molecular changes in CRC by determining the effect of specific molecular targets ref [23]. Chemical induced-CRC animal model is one of the most commonly CRC models, in which CAC model is usually induced by AOM/DSS to study the mechanism of inflammation related-tumorigenesis and development. The CRC model with TCM syndrome is an artificial disease and syndrome experimental animal model created by simulating and replicating characteristics of human disease prototype according to TCM theory ref [28]. An animal model combining with CRC and TCM syndromes might be useful to mimic the clinical characteristics of CRC patients with TCM syndrome ref [28]. Mouse is the commonly used to the models mentioned above ref [28], however, it is increasingly accepted that the use of larger animal models, especially dogs and pigs, can provide deeper insights in cancer research.
